documents: Abermann & Langley 2022, Permafrost and Periglacial Processes 33:129-133, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: It therefore appears appropriate to challenge the limited knowledge on the spatial coverage of RGs in Greenland.

steps.action: The authors take from Humlum's compilation and the near-global inventory (Jones et al.) that the southernmost known west-coast rock glacier lies near Sisimiut, and that the Greenland estimates are extrapolated from limited studies.
steps.quote: the southernmost known RG on the west coast occurs at around

steps.action: The authors pose the question whether the published southern limit of active rock glaciers in West Greenland holds.
steps.quote: It therefore appears appropriate to challenge the limited knowledge on the spatial coverage of RGs in Greenland.

steps.action: The authors identified BJRG in 2015 near Nuuk, described its morphology (ridges, furrows, slopes below 20°, a block-size transition), and recorded AWS air temperatures for 2016-2021 and spring water temperatures in 2016 and 2021.
steps.quote: where in 2015 we identified an RG—hereafter BJRG for Bjørneø RG—as a landscape feature

steps.action: The authors designed a network of spray-painted crosses on and around BJRG, to serve both as UAV ground control points and as displacement markers, and remeasured it by DGPS/GNSS in 2017, 2019 and 2021 (accuracy better than 2.5 cm).
steps.quote: we placed the crosses on and around BJRG

steps.action: The authors adopt the published expectation that bottom temperature of snow (BTS) indicates the likelihood of permafrost.
steps.quote: BTS has previously been used to estimate the likelihood of permafrost.

steps.action: The authors designed a BTS survey of 27 points on and around the rock glacier near maximum snow depth, with a probe-mounted sensor read until equilibrium; point placement was limited by accessibility.
steps.quote: measured 27 individual points distributed across the RG and its surroundings

steps.action: In August 2017 the authors observed compacted snow persisting in furrows, possibly due to cooling from below.
steps.quote: we observed compacted snow in several furrows that may have remained in place for the entire summer season

steps.action: The authors derived mean annual and total horizontal surface displacements of the GCPs for 2016-2021 and 2017-2019; all were below 3 cm/yr.
steps.quote: In general, surface motion is very small for all points (<3 cm/yr)

steps.action: The authors compared the displacements with the DGPS uncertainty: GCPs 7 and 8 moved northwest (downslope) beyond the uncertainty, while the other points stayed within it.
steps.quote: GCPs 7 and 8 show a horizontal displacement toward the northwest (downward flow) that is clearly beyond the uncertainties of the DGPS acquisition

steps.action: The authors measured BTS at 27 points in the March 2017 campaign and mapped the values.
steps.quote: the relative distribution of BTS during a winter campaign from March 28, 2017 reveals interesting patterns

steps.action: Using relative rather than absolute thresholds, the authors compared BTS on the rock glacier with BTS in its surroundings and found markedly lower values on the rock glacier.
steps.quote: on the BJRG they were significantly lower with values reaching

steps.action: The authors checked whether snow depth explains BTS and found a slight anticorrelation, too variable to be significant.
steps.quote: There was a slight anticorrelation where deeper snow cover showed slightly lower temperatures, but the variability was too large to draw significant conclusions.

steps.action: The authors take expected creep rates from the literature: sub-meter creep at slopes below 20° (Cicoira et al.) and low velocities at other high-latitude sites (Ødegård et al.).
steps.quote: They find very low (sub-meter) creep for slope angles <20

steps.action: The authors compared the BJRG velocities and slopes with these expectations and read the BTS contrast as support for an ice body.
steps.quote: The strong BTS differences between the RG and its immediate surroundings lend credence to an ice body below.

steps.action: The authors keep the claim of an active rock glacier at about 64°30'N, about 230 km south of the previous limit, as plausible and as a first assessment.
steps.quote: several independent indicators pointing towards the existence of an active RG

steps.action: The authors cite Rasch's qualitative remote-sensing candidates near the site (Figure S1) and note that this approach cannot assess activity.
steps.quote: the qualitative approach does not allow us to assess the activity state of the RGs

steps.action: The authors pose next questions for ice content (ERT, GPR), genesis and age (dating), a Greenland-wide inventory, and SAR-based activity assessment.
steps.quote: An important next step will be the deployment of additional geophysical methods

end.claim: Several independent indicators (downslope motion beyond DGPS uncertainty, low BTS relative to the surroundings, persistent furrow snow, cold springs) point to an active rock glacier at about 64°30'N, potentially extending the southern limit of active rock glaciers in West Greenland about 230 km south.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the repeated DGPS displacements with the measurement uncertainty, which shows downslope motion beyond the uncertainty at GCPs 7 and 8, is what makes the landform active rather than merely present.

gates.evidence: Action: after identifying the landform in 2015, the authors placed the GCP network in 2016 partly to determine surface displacement and ran the BTS survey to assess permafrost, but no explicit hypothesis is stated (p. 130). Claim: the displacement could have stayed within the ±2.5 cm uncertainty and BTS could have shown no contrast, so the claim could have failed; but only 2 of 8 points exceed the uncertainty, and the BTS reading is relative, with no threshold set (p. 130). Registration: nothing was reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: UAV-derived orthophoto; crosses used as UAV ground control points

novelty_claims.quote: we provide evidence for an active RG in West Greenland, about 230 km south of what previously has been identified as the southern limit of [...]
We present first monitoring results based on 5 years of air temperature near the RG snout
[...] provides a first assessment of an active RG

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Composition is none_fits: this is a single-site observational case report in which converging, independently measured indicators support a plausibility claim; no rivals are stated, there is no crucial test, and there is no repetition across sites (trace_series is the closest fit but needs past traces and stated rivals). Rival explanations (an inactive or relict rock glacier, perennial snow patches, a debris-covered or protalus landform, solifluction) are not discussed. The motion signal exceeds the DGPS uncertainty at only 2 of 8 points (Figure 1). BTS comes from one campaign; the date is given as both March 27 (Methods) and March 28, 2017 (Results, Figure 2 caption), an internal inconsistency. Absolute BTS thresholds are disavowed and no statistical test of the on/off contrast is reported, though the text says 'significantly lower'. Ice content is not shown; ERT, GPR and dating are deferred. Data are available only on request. Sub-claims and their statuses: displacement rates <3 cm/yr with ±2.5 cm resolution (estimate_with_resolution); BTS contrast indicating an ice body (best_explanation); persistent furrow snow and cold springs (qualitative observations, no status). The outcome is coded kept rather than contradicted because the authors hedge ('potentially', 'plausibility') and the earlier statement was a 'southernmost known' location rather than a tested limit; this is an inference.

disagreements.target: Humlum's compilation of Greenland rock glaciers placing the southernmost known west-coast RG near Sisimiut (refs 6, 13, 14)
disagreements.support: Field evidence of downslope motion beyond DGPS uncertainty and a strong BTS contrast at a site about 230 km further south.
disagreements.quote: to challenge the hitherto postulated southern boundary of active RGs in West Greenland

disagreements.target: Jones et al. 2018 near-global rock glacier inventory (ref 3) for its Greenland estimate
disagreements.support: The paper argues the Greenland estimate rests on a spatially limited study and on extrapolation from the Randolph Glacier Inventory, and offers an unlisted active rock glacier as evidence.
disagreements.quote: have based their estimates for Greenland on the spatially limited study by Humlum6 and extrapolated based on the Randolph Glacier Inventory.

disagreements.target: Use of absolute BTS thresholds to determine permafrost (refs 17, 18)
disagreements.support: The authors use only the relative BTS distribution and state that absolute thresholds are questionable.
disagreements.quote: While absolute thresholds of BTS are questionable and other, more adequate measures to determine permafrost occurrence exist

disagreements.target: Rasch 2016 qualitative remote-sensing identification of rock glaciers in the Nuuk area
disagreements.support: The authors argue that qualitative image analysis cannot establish activity, which requires displacement data such as DGPS or SAR.
disagreements.quote: the qualitative approach does not allow us to assess the activity state of the RGs

alternatives_considered.chosen: Relative distribution of BTS (on the rock glacier versus its surroundings)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Absolute BTS thresholds; 'other, more adequate measures to determine permafrost occurrence'
alternatives_considered.reason: Absolute thresholds of BTS are questionable
Steep parts, complex surface features and large boulders made consistent transects difficult
